result: More than half (7 of 13) of Upton et al.'s PCR-validated candidates are chimera artifacts that could not have been generated by L1 mobilization. These chimeras originated from inactive L1 elements, misinterpreted junctions from distinct L1 elements, or lacked poly-A tails. Upton et al. did not perform full-length cloning validation on any insertion, which is necessary to distinguish true insertions from chimeras in single-cell sequencing.
evaluation: Claims C19-C27, C31-C32, C35, C47, C49, and C81-C83 provide converging evidence that chimera artifacts are prevalent in Upton et al.'s validated candidates. The sequence analysis documented in Supplementary file 1 (C19-C22, C47, C49) demonstrates specific features inconsistent with true L1 mobilization. The validation failure rate (C23-C26) and absence of full-length cloning (C31) further support the high false-positive rate. The established knowledge about chimera formation (C81-C83) provides mechanistic context.

result: Full-length cloning validation is the only definitive method to confirm bona fide L1 insertions in single cells, as it verifies both breakpoints are present in the same DNA molecule. MALBAC amplification produces short amplicons (0.5-1.5kb), precluding efficient validation of insertions longer than ~1.5 kb, which represent 15-30% of somatic L1 insertions.
evaluation: Claims C28-C30 establish the logical necessity of full-length cloning based on the structural differences between true insertions (two breakpoints) and chimeras (one breakpoint). Claims C33-C34 document MALBAC's technical limitations with appropriate citations. The inference that MALBAC is unsuitable for validating longer insertions is well-supported by the amplicon size data and comparison to insertion size distributions from cancer studies.

result: 97% of Upton et al.'s single-cell insertion calls were supported by only a single sequencing read, while 53% of gold-standard germline KNR insertions were detected with ≥3 reads. Only 0.4% of somatic candidates were detected with ≥3 reads, and only 0.04% were detected at both 5' and 3' junctions compared to 11% for KNR insertions. This dramatic difference in read count and junction detection distributions indicates the vast majority of somatic candidates are false-positives.
evaluation: Claims C36-C46 present a comprehensive comparison of read count and junction detection distributions between gold-standard KNR insertions and somatic candidates. The data shown in Figures 2A-B clearly demonstrate the bimodal distribution of true insertions versus the unimodal low-signal distribution of somatic candidates. The statistical analysis is sound, using germline KNR insertions as an appropriate internal control since they share sequence characteristics with somatic insertions. The >250-fold difference in junction detection rates (C45-C46) provides independent confirmation.

result: Applying a read count threshold of >2 reads optimizes sensitivity and specificity, maintaining 53% detection of true KNR insertions while excluding ~99.6% of false-positives. This filtering yields only 20 somatic candidates across 170 cells, of which 12 were chimeras upon sequence analysis. The remaining 8 candidates yield a sensitivity-corrected somatic insertion rate of 0.19 per cell, with no significant difference between cell types (p=0.98, ANOVA), and 95% of cells had no somatic insertions.
evaluation: Claims C50-C55 describe a methodologically sound approach to correcting the insertion rate. The read count threshold (C50) is justified by optimization of sensitivity/specificity using gold-standard KNR insertions. The sequential filtering (C51-C52) with manual sequence verification is appropriate. The rate calculation (C53) includes sensitivity correction, which is necessary given the dropout observed. The statistical test (C54) is appropriate for comparing rates across groups. The finding that 95% of cells lack insertions (C55) is consistent with the low overall rate.

result: The reanalysis supports a somatic L1 insertion frequency of approximately 0.2 events per cell, which is about fifty-fold lower than reported by Upton et al. This corrected rate is consistent with prior estimates from L1-IP (0.07±0.15, p=0.54) and whole-genome sequencing (0.18±0.47, p=0.37), confirming that L1 elements mobilize in some human neurons but L1 mosaicism is not ubiquitous.
evaluation: Claims C5-C8 and C56-C58 present the corrected rate estimate and its comparison to prior studies. The ~50-fold reduction (C6) is well-documented through the filtering analysis. The consistency across three independent methods (C56-C58) with non-significant p-values from ANOVA tests provides strong support for the corrected rate. The conclusion that L1 mobilization occurs but is not ubiquitous (C7-C8, C76) is appropriately constrained by the data. Claims C76-C78 effectively summarize the main findings.

result: A likely bona fide L1Hs insertion was identified in neuron #11 (12 reads) and glial cell #2 (6 reads) from individual 45. This insertion shows all hallmarks of true retrotransposition: both 5' and 3' junctions, a TSD, poly-A tail, and a 3' transduction tracing to a known KNR L1 on chromosome 2. The same insertion was detected in two additional glial cells with 2 reads each.
evaluation: Claims C59-C61 describe a specific candidate with multiple lines of evidence supporting its authenticity. The high read counts (12 and 6 reads) place it well above the threshold and among the highest-signal candidates. The presence of all expected sequence features (C60) documented in Supplementary file 1, including traceability to a known source element, provides strong validation. Detection in multiple cells (C61) indicates this is a clonal event occurring during development, which is biologically plausible.

result: MALBAC-amplified single cells show systematic ~1 kb peaks and troughs of genome amplification at scales <50 kb, which is inherent to MALBAC as the same pattern occurs in unrelated studies. This non-uniformity at the genomic scale of retrotransposons explains the low read counts of some true KNR insertions, the high allelic dropout, and lower overall genome coverage breadth compared to MDA.
evaluation: Claims C62-C68 present a comprehensive analysis of MALBAC performance at relevant genomic scales. The high-resolution coverage analysis (C64) shown in Figure 4A directly demonstrates the peaks and troughs. The comparison to Zong et al. data (C65) provides independent validation that this is inherent to MALBAC rather than specific to Upton et al.'s implementation. The contrast with MDA (C66) is clearly shown. The inferences about effects on detection (C67-C68) are logical consequences of the observed non-uniformity and are supported by the data in Figure 4—figure supplement 2A.

result: At larger genomic scales (~500 kb bins), individual MALBAC single cells from Upton et al. have significantly lower quality than both MALBAC cells from Zong et al. and MDA neurons. However, pooling all 92 neurons achieves quality comparable to Zong et al., indicating the low quality is due to stochastic factors preceding MALBAC (e.g., tissue quality) rather than MALBAC itself. Power spectral density analysis confirms MALBAC has better uniformity at large scales (>30 kb) but worse uniformity at small scales (<30 kb) compared to MDA, making MALBAC unsuitable for retrotransposon studies.
evaluation: Claims C69-C75 provide a multi-scale analysis of amplification quality. The low-resolution analysis (C69) with MAPD/MDAD metrics shown in Figure 4B and supplements provides quantitative evidence. The pooling analysis (C70) effectively distinguishes systematic MALBAC effects from sample-specific quality issues. The comparison of MALBAC and MDA at large scales (C71-C72) is supported by data and citations. The power spectral density analysis (C73) provides comprehensive scale-dependent characterization. The conclusions about method suitability (C74-C75) are well-supported by the scale-dependent performance data.

result: RC-seq bulk somatic candidates have a non-canonical distribution of large TSD sizes, inconsistent with nearly all prior L1 research.
evaluation: Claim C48 identifies an anomaly in the TSD size distribution that is inconsistent with established knowledge about L1 insertions. The analysis is documented in Appendix 1, and the finding is corroborated by C49 showing that randomly selected candidates with large TSDs were all chimeras. This provides independent evidence for the high false-positive rate.

result: The corrected RC-seq retrotransposition rate is consistent with rates measured in vitro in neuronal progenitors and with the absence of significant somatic L1 insertions in brain tumors.
evaluation: Claims C79-C80 place the corrected rate in broader biological context through comparison to other systems. The consistency with in vitro progenitor rates (C79) and brain tumor data (C80) is supported by appropriate citations. These comparisons strengthen confidence in the corrected rate by showing it aligns with independent observations from different experimental systems.

result: Single-cell genomics enables direct measurement of somatic mutation rates in human brain and has revealed previously unknown mutation mechanisms. L1 elements are retrotransposons that can mobilize in neuronal progenitor cells and create mutations. Prior studies using different methods reported disparate L1 mobilization rates, with bulk DNA studies suggesting higher rates than transgenic reporter studies. Single-cell sequencing was proposed as the definitive method to resolve these estimates.
evaluation: Claims C1 and C13-C14 describe the capabilities of single-cell sequencing, supported by multiple citations to prior work. Claims C9-C12 provide established background on L1 biology with appropriate citations. Claims C15-C18 accurately summarize the state of the field prior to the current study, documenting the discrepancy between methods and the proposed role of single-cell sequencing. All claims are well-supported by citations to relevant literature.
